rules: Answer the question first, then tell it as Situation, Task, Action, Result.
Speak for 2 to 4 minutes. Spend most of that time on what you did, the obstacle, and the tradeoff.
Put a metric in every result, with its baseline and unit.
Say I for your own work, and credit others accurately.
Use examples from the last 5 years. Every story here qualifies.
Each answer should show 4 to 6 Leadership Principles. The chips on each story show which.
Close with the lesson, then be ready for: How would you do this at AWS? What would you do differently?

beats.label: Who
beats.text: I'm Anuvik, an MS computer science student at USC graduating in December 2026. I spent nearly 3 years at Oracle working on observability, incident diagnostics, and Kubernetes for enterprise services.

beats.label: Proof
beats.text: One project reduced P1 MTTR from 94 to 26 minutes by giving on-call engineers diagnostic tags and runbook context.

beats.label: Customer
beats.text: At MSRcosmos, I built agentic ERP migration workflows with human review across 12 client entities, cutting turnaround from 3 days to 5.5 hours.

beats.label: Why SA
beats.text: That combination is what I want to bring to the AWSI-ETP Solutions Architect role: understand a customer challenge, compare AWS designs, and explain the recommendation clearly to engineers and executives.

pitch.closing_line: My focus is the customer outcome: a solution that solves the problem and can be operated reliably.

lps.name: Customer Obsession

lps.meaning: Act on behalf of the whole company and the long term; never say that is not my job.

lps.name: Bias for Action
lps.meaning: Speed matters; many decisions are reversible, so take calculated risks.

lps.name: Earn Trust
lps.meaning: Listen, speak candidly, admit mistakes, and treat others respectfully.

lps.name: Learn and Be Curious
lps.meaning: Never done learning; explore new possibilities.

lps.name: Insist on the Highest Standards
lps.meaning: Keep raising the bar; do not pass defects downstream.

lps.name: Deliver Results

lps.name: Dive Deep
lps.meaning: Stay connected to the details; no task is beneath you.

lps.name: Invent and Simplify
lps.meaning: Expect and find new ways; make the complex simple.

lps.name: Are Right, A Lot

lps.name: Hire and Develop the Best

lps.name: Frugality

stories.title: Multi-agent ERP migration with human-in-the-loop
stories.headline: I built an ERP migration workflow that cut turnaround from 3 days to 5.5 hours across 12 client entities.
stories.s: At MSRcosmos, I worked on moving 10,000+ financial records from Sage X3 to Sage Intacct across 12 client entities. The records covered the general ledger, accounts payable, and accounts receivable. Reconciliation created a substantial manual workload.
stories.t: My task was to automate that workflow while keeping a clear path for human review when a record needed attention.
a: I built the multi-agent workflow with the Claude API and LangGraph, and connected it to Sage REST APIs through MCP tool calling.

I designed confidence-based routing: records above the threshold could auto-approve, while lower-confidence records went to a reviewer. This focused human effort on exceptions rather than treating every record the same way.
I containerized the system with Docker for cloud-agnostic deployment across AWS, Azure, and GCP.
stories.r: Manual reconciliation fell 68%, and 83% of records auto-approved. Turnaround decreased from 3 days to 5.5 hours.
stories.lesson: The central design lesson is that useful automation needs an explicit boundary between what the system can process and what a person should review.
stories.twist: For engineers, explain confidence routing, independent validation, and safe replay. For executives, explain the reported turnaround from 3 days to 5.5 hours and the reviewer decision boundary. Confirm the measurement and stakeholder acceptance; do not claim audit compliance or zero errors.
stories.aws: Proposed AWS design, not a claim of AWS implementation: Bedrock running Claude for the agents, Step Functions Standard for state, retries, and the human-review wait (task token), S3 for staging, Lambda functions as tools, DynamoDB for the audit trail.

probes.q: How did you set the confidence threshold?
probes.a: The system used confidence-based routing: above the threshold a record auto-approved, and lower-confidence cases went to a reviewer. I would not quote a threshold or a precision figure without its calibration evidence. For evaluation, I would use expert-reviewed records and measure false approvals, review workload, and performance on different record types.

probes.q: What happened when the model was confidently wrong?
probes.a: Confidence is not proof of correctness. The implemented workflow had a human-review path for lower-confidence records. To address confidently wrong outputs in an AWS design, I would add deterministic financial checks, sample auto-approved records for review, and use errors to refine the routing policy. I would distinguish those proposed controls from what I can substantiate about this implementation.

probes.q: What did it cost per record?
probes.a: I can speak to the operational results: 68% less manual reconciliation and turnaround from 3 days to 5.5 hours. I would not turn those into a dollar saving without cost data. For a cost model, I would include model calls, tokens, runtime, storage, and reviewer time per record.

probes.q: How would you build it on AWS only?
probes.a: I would use a supported Claude model on Bedrock, S3 for staging, and Step Functions Standard to coordinate processing and wait for human review through a callback. Lambda could expose the tools, DynamoDB could store workflow decisions, and CloudWatch would monitor the system. I would design permissions, idempotency, timeouts, and financial validation before choosing an auto-approval policy.

stories.evidence_note: Resume-supported actions and metrics are candidate claims, not independently verified. See the resume and STAR review.

long.stakes: A wrong entry changes what a client believes it owes or is owed, and each of the 12 entities ran on its own cloud. Slow reconciliation also held back the move to the new system.
long.obstacle: The hard part was trust. A finance team will not accept a black box that approves its ledger. [fill: the moment or record type that made this clear, for example a class of records the agent kept getting wrong]
long.tradeoff: The threshold was the real decision. Set it high and reviewers drown in records the system could have handled. Set it low and wrong records slip through. In finance a missed error costs far more than an extra review, so I treated the threshold as a dial backed by reviewed results. [fill: where you set it first and how you adjusted it]
long.buy_in: [fill: who had to accept the auto-approval rule, for example the client finance lead, and what evidence convinced them, such as reviewed sample records side by side]
long.result: Manual reconciliation fell 68%. 83% of records cleared automatically above the threshold, so reviewers spent their time on the records that needed judgment. Turnaround went from 3 days to 5.5 hours across the 12 entities.
long.different: I would build the evaluation set first: records reviewed by an expert before launch, so the threshold rests on a measured false-approval rate from day one. I would also add deterministic accounting checks, such as debits equal credits, that run no matter how confident the model is.
long.at_aws: On AWS I would run Claude on Amazon Bedrock for the agents and use AWS Step Functions to coordinate the steps and pause for human review with a callback. Amazon S3 would hold staged records, AWS Lambda functions would be the tools, and Amazon DynamoDB would keep an audit trail of every decision. Amazon Bedrock Guardrails and least-privilege IAM roles would limit what the agents can touch.

stories.title: P1 MTTR from 94 to 26 minutes
stories.headline: I reduced P1 incident recovery time at Oracle from 94 to 26 minutes by putting diagnostic context in front of on-call engineers.
stories.s: At Oracle, I worked on NSX observability for a platform serving 37,000+ enterprise tenants. During an incident, detecting an API failure is only the starting point; the engineer still needs to understand the likely cause and the next action.
stories.t: My work was to improve that diagnosis path through real-time API diagnostics across 1M+ endpoints.
a: I instrumented the high-throughput event streams so API failure evidence was available in real time.
I added automatic root-cause tags for 400- and 500-series failures, connecting the failure signal with useful diagnostic context.

I included runbook context so the on-call engineer could move from seeing an error to investigating and mitigating it. The important change was making the information actionable, rather than simply producing more telemetry.
stories.r: P1 MTTR dropped from 94 to 26 minutes, a 72% reduction.
stories.lesson: The lesson is that operational tooling should shorten the path from signal to action. A dashboard has value when it helps someone recover the service.
stories.twist: For engineers, explain the actual event signals, tag logic, false diagnoses, and rollout. For executives, explain recovery from 94 to 26 minutes and the affected customer workflow. Confirm the measurement and impact; a P1 does not establish every customer was down.
stories.aws: Proposed AWS design, not a claim of AWS implementation: CloudWatch Logs Insights and metric filters, X-Ray traces, EventBridge rules to tag and route, Systems Manager Automation runbooks attached to alarms.

probes.q: Which signals drove the tags?
probes.a: I instrumented real-time API diagnostics on event streams and used automatic root-cause tags for 400- and 500-series failures, with runbook context for on-call engineers. The tag gives the engineer an investigation starting point. For a new design, I would correlate status codes with request and service context and recent changes, because a status code alone does not establish the root cause.

probes.q: Rules or a model?
probes.a: My contribution was API instrumentation, automatic root-cause tagging, and runbook context. That result does not depend on presenting the tagger as machine learning. For a new implementation, I would start with explainable rules for known failure patterns, measure incorrect tags, and add a model only if evaluation showed a useful improvement.

probes.q: How was MTTR measured, and over what window?
probes.a: P1 MTTR went from 94 to 26 minutes. To give the exact incident count and comparison window, I would need the underlying incident-tracker data. A defensible comparison uses consistent incident-start and recovery definitions, comparable severity and workload, and accounts for other operational changes. The metric supports the recovery result; it does not establish that diagnostics were the only contributor.

probes.q: What is a limitation of automatic root-cause tagging?
probes.a: A root-cause tag is a hypothesis, not proof. The engineer needs supporting evidence and runbook context so they can verify it and continue investigating if it is wrong. For a new system, I would evaluate incorrect tags, missing tags, and time to a useful action, rather than optimize only the number of failures labeled.

stories.evidence_note: Resume-supported actions and metrics are candidate claims, not independently verified. See the resume and STAR review.

long.stakes: A P1 is the highest severity, so every minute of one is time enterprise customers may feel. The slow part was diagnosis: knowing an API was failing did not tell on-call why.
long.obstacle: The evidence existed, but it was spread across high-throughput event streams from 1M+ endpoints. [fill: the specific obstacle, for example event noise, who owned the streams, or the cost of tagging in real time]
long.tradeoff: I focused on the failures that could be tagged with confidence, the 400 and 500 series, instead of trying to diagnose everything. A wrong tag sends on-call down the wrong path, so each tag came with its evidence and runbook context, and the engineer kept the final call.
long.buy_in: [fill: how on-call engineers or the team lead came to use the tags, for example a trial on one service first]
long.result: P1 mean time to recovery dropped from 94 to 26 minutes, a 72% reduction. On-call started each incident with a likely cause and the runbook step instead of a blank screen.
long.different: I would measure tag accuracy from day one: how often each tag was right, wrong, or missing. That proves the tags drove the faster recovery and shows which tags to retire.
long.at_aws: On AWS I would use Amazon CloudWatch Logs and metric filters for the error signals, AWS X-Ray traces to see which service failed, Amazon EventBridge rules to tag and route events, and AWS Systems Manager Automation runbooks attached to CloudWatch alarms, so the first step of the fix is one click.

stories.title: SLO alerting, 41% fewer false pages
stories.headline: I reduced false-positive on-call pages by 41% by improving the observability and alerting approach at Oracle.
stories.s: The NSX environment served 37,000+ enterprise tenants. Static thresholds can produce pages when a resource crosses a limit without clearly explaining whether the service is meeting its objectives. That makes alert quality as important as alert coverage.
stories.t: I architected the Prometheus and Grafana observability stack and moved alerting toward service-level objectives, using CPU, memory, and p99 latency signals.
a: I organized the monitoring around the service objectives and the signals engineers needed to investigate degradation.
I built 47 dashboards and alert rules across the observability stack. Dashboards provided the investigation view, while alert rules determined when an engineer needed to take action.
I treated the resource signals and latency together: CPU or memory alone does not describe the entire experience of a service.
stories.lesson: The design lesson is to make alerts actionable and tied to service behavior. Reducing noise only helps if the system still brings meaningful problems to the on-call engineer.
stories.twist: For engineers, explain the actual SLI, target, alert sensitivity, and missed-incident checks. For executives, connect 41% fewer false-positive pages to attention available for real incidents, without claiming measured productivity or customer benefit that was not recorded.
stories.aws: Proposed AWS design, not a claim of AWS implementation: Amazon Managed Service for Prometheus and Amazon Managed Grafana, CloudWatch Application Signals SLOs, composite alarms to cut noise.

probes.q: How did you pick the targets?
probes.a: The stack moved toward SLO-based alerting with CPU, memory, and p99 latency signals. I would distinguish resource metrics from the actual service objective rather than treat them as interchangeable. When defining a new SLO, I would start with the customer-facing operation, its acceptable latency or availability, and the reliability tradeoff the stakeholders can accept.

probes.q: How did you handle cardinality across 37,000+ tenants?
probes.a: The monitoring scope covered 37,000+ tenants; that scope does not mean every metric had a tenant label. For a new design, I would aggregate the operational view by useful service dimensions and use controlled queries for detailed tenant investigation. Labels need a deliberate budget, because an unbounded combination of tenants, endpoints, and request identifiers can make the monitoring system costly and difficult to operate.

probes.q: Did you use burn-rate alerting?
probes.a: The implementation moved toward SLO-based alerting and reduced false-positive pages by 41%. I would need the original alert configuration to describe the exact burn-rate policy. For a new design, I would consider multi-window burn-rate alerts to distinguish rapid error-budget consumption from slower degradation, then test whether the alerts produce an actionable response.

stories.evidence_note: Resume-supported actions and metrics are candidate claims, not independently verified. See the resume and STAR review.

long.stakes: Every false page wakes an engineer for nothing. After enough of them, people trust alerts less, and that is how a real incident gets missed. Across 37,000+ tenants, alert noise was a reliability risk, not just an annoyance.
long.obstacle: Static thresholds felt safe because they were familiar. [fill: the pushback you got, for example a worry that SLO alerts would miss real problems, and how you answered it]
long.tradeoff: Fewer alerts carries a risk: you might miss something. So alerts followed what customers feel, p99 latency against the objective, while CPU and memory became investigation signals on dashboards instead of pages.
long.buy_in: [fill: how you showed the team the new alerts still caught real incidents, for example running both alert sets side by side for a while]
long.result: False-positive pages fell 41%. I built 47 dashboards and alert rules, so the engineer who did get paged had the view to act on it.
long.different: I would publish an error budget for each service, so teams could see how much reliability they had left and make release decisions with it.
long.at_aws: On AWS I would keep the same tooling with Amazon Managed Service for Prometheus and Amazon Managed Grafana, define SLOs in Amazon CloudWatch Application Signals, and use CloudWatch composite alarms so one problem fires one page instead of five.

stories.title: CLI validation toolchain adopted by 4 teams
stories.headline: I shipped a validation toolchain adopted by 4 teams that reduced failed deployments from 11% to 4%.
stories.s: At Oracle, configuration errors could be discovered during deployment or after a change reached production. Finding the same issue earlier in the delivery process gives engineers a chance to correct it before it becomes an operational problem.
stories.t: My task was to build scripted pre-deployment validation into the Jenkins CI/CD workflow.
a: I shipped a CLI toolchain that ran the validation checks as part of CI, so configuration problems could fail before the deployment stage.
I made the checks part of the delivery workflow rather than leaving validation as an informal step an engineer had to remember.
The toolchain was adopted by 4 engineering teams across NSX. That gave multiple teams a common way to catch configuration errors earlier while continuing to use Jenkins for delivery.
stories.r: Release cycles became 34% shorter, and the failed-deployment rate fell from 11% to 4%.
stories.lesson: The lesson is that reliability can improve developer speed. A useful validation mechanism prevents downstream rework and makes the safer path part of the normal workflow.
stories.twist: For engineers, demonstrate one pre-deployment check and its exception policy. For executives, explain failed deploys falling from 11% to 4% and release cycles 34% shorter. Confirm attribution and adoption actions before presenting this as a customer-influence example.
stories.aws: Proposed AWS design, not a claim of AWS implementation: CodePipeline with a CodeBuild validation stage, cfn-lint and CloudFormation Guard for templates, AWS Config rules for drift.

probes.q: What made the validation useful across teams?
probes.a: The common value was catching configuration errors in the Jenkins workflow before deployment. Four NSX teams adopted the toolchain, release cycles became 34% shorter, and failed deployments fell from 11% to 4%. For a customer-facing design, I would evaluate the same adoption tradeoff: useful protection with clear errors and an explicit exception policy, balanced against build time and false rejections.

probes.q: How did you handle team-specific needs?
probes.a: The implementation was a Jenkins CLI toolchain with scripted pre-deployment validation, adopted by 4 NSX teams. The team-specific extension mechanism would require the original implementation details. In a new design, I would separate shared checks from team policy, return actionable errors, and make exceptions explicit so customization does not silently disable the safeguards.

probes.q: How large was the deployment improvement?
probes.a: The failed-deployment rate went from 11% to 4%, a decrease of 7 percentage points. That is different from saying a 7% relative reduction. Four teams adopted the toolchain, and release cycles became 34% shorter. Those are separate measures of adoption, deployment reliability, and delivery time; none by itself demonstrates mentoring or a particular persuasion tactic.

stories.evidence_note: Resume-supported actions and metrics are candidate claims, not independently verified. See the resume and STAR review.

long.stakes: 11% of deployments were failing. Each failure meant a rollback, a rerun, and engineers pulled off planned work, and some configuration errors only surfaced after a change reached production.
long.obstacle: A gate that slows teams down gets bypassed. [fill: the hardest adoption obstacle, for example a team worried about build time or false rejections]
long.tradeoff: Every check adds build time. The tradeoff is seconds in the pipeline against a failed deploy later, so each check had to catch a real class of error, and each failure message had to say exactly what to fix. [fill: one concrete check the toolchain ran]
long.buy_in: I started with [fill: the first team or service], then used its results to bring the next teams on. 4 teams across NSX adopted it.
long.result: Failed deploys fell from 11% to 4%, and release cycles got 34% shorter.
long.different: I would record which check caught what. That data shows which checks earn their place, and it makes the case to the next team in one chart.
long.at_aws: On AWS I would build this into AWS CodePipeline with an AWS CodeBuild validation stage, run cfn-lint and AWS CloudFormation Guard on templates, and use AWS Config rules to catch drift after deployment.

stories.title: NetSuite search latency down 30%
stories.headline: I reduced NetSuite search P50 page-load latency from 840 milliseconds to 588 milliseconds, a 30% reduction.
stories.s: At Oracle, I worked on search performance at enterprise data volumes. A slow page can have several causes, so the important starting point was to understand how the database was executing the queries behind the search.
stories.t: My task was to improve the database access path driving that page-load latency.
a: I profiled the query plans to identify the SQL responsible for full scans.
I restructured indexes on the hot predicates and rewrote the SQL driving those scans. The goal was to make the access path better match the filters the search actually used.
I focused on the query plan and index design because reducing unnecessary reads addresses the work the database is doing, rather than assuming that a larger instance is the answer.
stories.r: P50 page-load latency improved from 840 to 588 milliseconds, a 30% reduction in median page load through a better database access path.
stories.lesson: The lesson is to diagnose the access pattern before selecting a scaling solution. The right architecture recommendation starts with evidence about the bottleneck.
stories.twist: For engineers, explain one query plan, index choice, write cost, and rollout. For executives, explain median search page load falling from 840 ms to 588 ms and ask which user workflow matters. Do not invent hardware savings or increased revenue.
stories.aws: Proposed AWS design, not a claim of AWS implementation: RDS or Aurora with CloudWatch Database Insights and EXPLAIN plans; indexes first, then read replicas or ElastiCache, a bigger instance last. See https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonCloudWatch/latest/monitoring/Database-Insights.html; verify engine and Region support.

probes.q: How did you find the hot predicates?
probes.a: I profiled the query plans and restructured indexes on hot predicates in the SQL driving full scans. The useful technical question is whether the access path matches the filters and data distribution. I would examine plan shape, estimated versus actual rows, selectivity, and the frequency of the relevant query before recommending an index.

probes.q: Did the new indexes slow writes?
probes.a: The measured result I can give is the P50 page-load reduction from 840 to 588 milliseconds. I would not claim a write-latency result that I cannot substantiate. An index adds write and storage work, so I would evaluate insert and update latency, index size, and workload balance alongside the read improvement.

probes.q: How would you roll out the query changes safely?
probes.a: My implementation work was query-plan profiling, index restructuring, and SQL changes. For a production rollout, I would verify result correctness on representative data, compare read and write behavior, inspect tail latency, and check locking implications for the database engine. I would also define how to revert the query or index change before exposing the full workload.

stories.evidence_note: Resume-supported actions and metrics are candidate claims, not independently verified. See the resume and STAR review.

long.stakes: Search is something users touch all day. At 840 milliseconds median, every search felt slow. The easy answer, a bigger database instance, would have cost more every month without proving it fixed the cause.
long.obstacle: [fill: what made the diagnosis hard, for example queries that were only slow at certain data volumes]
long.tradeoff: Indexes speed up reads but slow down writes and take space. So I restructured indexes on the hot predicates, the filters the searches actually used, instead of indexing everything.
long.buy_in: [fill: who reviewed the index and SQL changes, and how you showed they were safe, for example before and after query plans]
long.result: Median page load fell from 840 to 588 milliseconds, 30% faster, from a better access path rather than bigger hardware.
long.different: I would add query performance checks to the release process, so a new query that triggers a full scan is caught before users feel it.
long.at_aws: On Amazon RDS or Amazon Aurora I would start with Performance Insights to find the top queries by load, read their EXPLAIN plans, and fix indexes and SQL before resizing anything. If reads still dominate, I would add read replicas or an Amazon ElastiCache layer.

stories.title: Kubernetes autoscaling on custom metrics
stories.headline: I used custom-metric autoscaling on OCI to keep NSX services within their p99 latency objectives at 2x peak load.
stories.s: At Oracle, release surges created changing demand for NSX services. Keeping the services responsive required both containerized deployment and a scaling policy that reflected the workload, rather than looking only at CPU utilization.
stories.t: My work combined Docker and Kubernetes containerization with horizontal autoscaling driven by custom Prometheus metrics.
a: I containerized the NSX services on OCI using Docker and Kubernetes.

I used custom Prometheus metrics as inputs to horizontal autoscaling instead of relying on CPU alone. Resource utilization is useful, but it is not a complete explanation of whether a service is keeping up with its demand.
I connected the scaling behavior to the service latency objective, keeping the discussion focused on the performance the system needed to preserve through a surge.
stories.r: The services held their p99 SLOs at 2x peak load through release surges.
stories.lesson: The lesson is to scale from a signal that represents the workload and to evaluate the result against a service objective. My implementation experience here was on OCI.
stories.twist: For engineers, trace the actual metric through replica demand, node capacity, readiness, and stabilization. For executives, describe holding p99 objectives at 2x peak load, with the test conditions confirmed. Distinguish OCI experience from a proposed EKS or ECS design.
stories.aws: Proposed AWS design, not a claim of AWS implementation: EKS with HPA on custom metrics (Prometheus adapter or KEDA), Karpenter for nodes; or ECS service auto scaling with target tracking.

probes.q: Which metric, and why not CPU?
probes.a: I used custom Prometheus metrics instead of relying on CPU alone. The precise signal and target would need to come from the autoscaler configuration. The reason to go beyond CPU is that it can miss a workload bottleneck. For a new design, I would test whether queue depth, in-flight requests, or another service signal predicts saturation and latency for that application.

probes.q: How would you handle scale-up lag on AWS?
probes.a: The OCI implementation held p99 SLOs at 2x peak load. In an AWS design, I would account separately for detecting demand, adding replicas, obtaining node capacity, and becoming ready to serve traffic. I would measure the total delay against the service objective and test whether scaling capacity arrives before the workload saturates.

probes.q: How did you prevent flapping?
probes.a: I would not quote stabilization settings without the actual autoscaler configuration. In a new design, I would use a stable workload signal, tune the observation and stabilization periods, and scale down conservatively. I would test oscillating demand and dependency limits, because rapid replica changes can create instability rather than solve it.

stories.evidence_note: Resume-supported actions and metrics are candidate claims, not independently verified. See the resume and STAR review.

long.stakes: Release surges pushed load well above normal. If the services fell behind, p99 latency would break its objective for tenants at exactly the moment changes were rolling out.
long.obstacle: CPU could look healthy while latency was not. [fill: when you saw CPU-based scaling react too late]
long.tradeoff: Scaling on custom metrics takes more work to set up and tune than scaling on CPU. I accepted that because CPU alone was not the signal that tracked whether the service kept up.
long.buy_in: [fill: how you validated the scaling policy before production, for example a load test at peak]
long.result: The services held their p99 SLOs at 2x peak load through release surges.
long.different: I would add cost tracking next to the latency objective, so we know both that we stayed fast and what staying fast cost.
long.at_aws: On AWS I would run Amazon EKS with the Kubernetes Horizontal Pod Autoscaler on custom metrics from Amazon Managed Service for Prometheus, add node capacity with Karpenter, and alarm in CloudWatch on p99 latency.

stories.title: Applying LangGraph and MCP to the ERP workflow
stories.headline: I applied LangGraph orchestration and MCP tool calling to make an ERP migration workflow work across model, API, and human-review steps.
stories.s: At MSRcosmos, the migration from Sage X3 to Sage Intacct involved financial records and multiple kinds of processing. A model response alone could not complete the workflow: the application also needed to interact with business systems and route records for review.
stories.t: My task was to connect those capabilities into the multi-agent migration system.
a: I used the Claude API with LangGraph for the agent workflow, giving the orchestration a defined place in the application rather than treating the entire task as a single model response.
I connected Sage REST APIs through MCP tool calling so the workflow could interact with the ERP systems.
I combined that integration with confidence-based human review and Docker packaging for cloud-agnostic deployment. These pieces addressed different parts of delivering a usable application.
stories.r: The migration system reduced manual reconciliation by 68%.
stories.lesson: The lesson is that learning a framework matters when it helps solve an application problem. Orchestration, tools, and review each have a distinct responsibility in a working system.
stories.twist: For engineers, describe a real learning experiment and how it changed the implementation. For executives, explain why learning reduced delivery uncertainty only if you can substantiate that connection. This is another angle on S1, not a separate customer result.
stories.aws: Proposed AWS design, not a claim of AWS implementation: Same pattern for a new AWS service: read the quotas and pricing pages, build a small hands-on prototype, then learn its failure modes.

probes.q: What did LangGraph and MCP each contribute?
probes.a: LangGraph was part of the agent orchestration, while MCP tool calling connected the workflow with Sage REST APIs. The distinction matters: orchestration coordinates the application work, and tools provide a controlled way to interact with external systems. The human-review layer handled cases outside the auto-approval path.

probes.q: How would you learn an unfamiliar AWS service?
probes.a: I would start with the customer requirement, then read the service documentation for its operating model, quotas, security boundaries, pricing, and failure modes. I would build a small representative workflow, observe its behavior, and compare it with a simpler alternative. The goal would be to understand when the service fits, not just make a demonstration run.

stories.note: Same ERP episode as S1, told from the orchestration angle. Do not count it as a separate customer engagement or a documented rapid-learning timeline.
stories.evidence_note: Resume-supported actions and metrics are candidate claims, not independently verified. See the resume and STAR review.

long.stakes: The migration could not be done with one model prompt. The workflow had to call business systems, keep state across steps, and stop for a human. I had to learn the tools that make that possible while delivering a client project.
long.obstacle: [fill: what was new to you, for example LangGraph state graphs or MCP servers, and how you learned it: docs, small prototypes, examples]
long.tradeoff: A framework adds structure and also a dependency. I used LangGraph where orchestration and state needed it, and kept the Sage API calls behind MCP tools so each piece could be tested on its own.
long.buy_in: [fill: how you showed the team the approach worked, for example a demo on one entity]
long.result: The system cut manual reconciliation by 68%.
long.different: I would write a short guide while learning, so the next engineer ramps up faster.
long.at_aws: On AWS I would host the agents on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore with a Claude model from Amazon Bedrock, expose each business system as an AWS Lambda tool, and keep long-running workflow state and the human-review pause in AWS Step Functions.

stories.title: DQN training stall, 40% shorter runs
stories.note: USC Sports Analytics is volunteer research. Say so plainly; do not call it an internship.
stories.headline: I shortened DQN training runs from 52 to 31 minutes by fixing replay-buffer sampling and a data-loader stall.
stories.s: In sports analytics research at USC, I prototyped a reinforcement-learning agent for NFL fourth-down decisions using 420K plays. The agent used expected points added in its reward design, and each training run took 52 minutes.
stories.t: My work included improving the training pipeline so each experiment spent less time on data handling.
a: I vectorized replay-buffer sampling, moving that work away from inefficient per-item processing.
I removed a data-loader stall. Both changes targeted the path feeding training rather than changing the problem into a request for more compute.
I kept the performance result separate from the model-quality result: making the pipeline quicker and improving decision agreement are different accomplishments with different measurements.
stories.r: Training time fell to 31 minutes per run, about a 40% reduction in runtime. Separately, agreement with EPA-optimal calls improved from 68% to 74% on held-out 2024 drives.
stories.lesson: The lesson is to understand the work surrounding model computation. Data movement and sampling can limit experiment speed even when the model itself gets most of the attention.
stories.twist: For engineers, explain sampling vectorization, the loader stall, and equivalent-workload checks. For executives, explain runs shortening from 52 to 31 minutes without claiming measured cost savings. Keep the separate quality change and research context explicit.
stories.aws: Proposed AWS design, not a claim of AWS implementation: SageMaker AI training jobs with Profiler and Debugger; Spot training for cheaper runs.

probes.q: How would you isolate the same training bottleneck?
probes.a: The changes were vectorized replay-buffer sampling and removal of a data-loader stall. To isolate that class of bottleneck, I would time sampling, data transfer, and model computation separately and compare utilization with the wall-clock time spent in each stage. The aim is to distinguish waiting for input from computing the model, then optimize the stage that dominates runtime.

probes.q: How do the runtime and quality results differ?
probes.a: Runtime fell from 52 to 31 minutes, about 40% less time per run. Separately, agreement with EPA-optimal calls increased from 68% to 74%, a gain of 6 percentage points. I do not attribute the quality gain to faster data handling. To verify an optimization preserves training behavior, I would compare sampling semantics, training curves, and held-out results under controlled conditions.

stories.evidence_note: Resume-supported actions and metrics are candidate claims, not independently verified. See the resume and STAR review.

long.stakes: Each training run took 52 minutes, which capped how many experiments fit in a day. In research, iteration speed decides how fast you learn.
long.obstacle: The model code looked fine; the time was going somewhere else. [fill: how you found it, for example a profiler showing the GPU idle while the data loader waited]
long.tradeoff: I could have asked for more compute. I profiled first instead, because more compute does not fix a pipeline that is waiting on data.
long.buy_in: [fill: how you shared the fix with the research group]
long.result: Runs dropped from 52 to 31 minutes, about 40%. Separately, agreement with EPA-optimal calls rose from 68% to 74% on held-out 2024 drives. I keep those apart: one is speed, the other is model quality.
long.different: I would profile the first run, not wait until runs became painful.
long.at_aws: On AWS I would use Amazon SageMaker AI training jobs with built-in profiling to spot an idle GPU, and stage the training data in Amazon S3 in the same Region as the training instances.

stories.title: PacSun executive intelligence app
stories.headline: I am building a retail intelligence application that turns operational context into an owner-tagged view and briefs for PacSun executives.
stories.s: At USC Annenberg, my work is a multi-agent application on Claude Enterprise for an executive audience. The application needs to bring together context from internal systems and present it in a form that supports decisions.
stories.t: My task is to connect that context with ranked operational issues, clear owners, and useful executive outputs.
a: I am wiring MCP connectors into internal systems so the agents can pull live context.

I am building the workflow that ranks operational issues into an owner-tagged view and drafts CEO briefs. The presentation puts the issue and its owner together instead of making the executive reconstruct the connection.
I also engineered a scheduling workflow that ranks open issues by urgency and owner, then proposes meeting slots with agendas.
stories.r: The work is ongoing. The application brings context gathering, issue ranking, brief drafting, and meeting proposals into a workflow for executive decision-making.
stories.lesson: The lesson is that executive communication is part of the solution design. Information becomes useful when the audience can see what needs attention and who owns the next step.
stories.twist: For engineers, explain connector permissions, source attribution, ranking evaluation, and approval. For executives, explain which decision the owner-tagged view supports. State what is live and what remains a prototype; measured adoption or business impact is not yet supplied.
stories.aws: Proposed AWS design, not a claim of AWS implementation: Amazon Bedrock AgentCore with Lambda tools in place of MCP connectors, Knowledge Bases for documents, Guardrails, and IAM-scoped access to each system.

probes.q: How do agents get live data safely?
probes.a: The application uses MCP connectors into internal systems. For the security design, I would scope each connector to the tools and data needed, preserve the requesting user context where required, and distinguish read access from actions that change a system. I would not assume that using MCP by itself provides authorization.

probes.q: How do you stop a wrong brief from reaching the CEO?
probes.a: The app drafts briefs; drafting should be separated from approval and delivery. For that control path, I would require source attribution, check important claims against retrieved records, and route the draft through an accountable reviewer. I would evaluate factual errors on representative briefs rather than assume fluent text is reliable.

probes.q: Why several agents instead of one?
probes.a: The application brings together context gathering, issue ranking, brief drafting, and meeting proposals. Those responsibilities provide a useful way to reason about the workflow. I would still compare the orchestration with a simpler implementation, because more agents also add latency, cost, and coordination failures. The design needs evidence that the extra complexity helps.

stories.evidence_note: Resume-supported actions and metrics are candidate claims, not independently verified. See the resume and STAR review.

long.stakes: Executives decide based on what reaches them. If the right issue and the right owner do not reach them together, decisions wait.
long.obstacle: [fill: the hardest part so far, for example reliable live context from internal systems, or agreeing what urgent means]
long.tradeoff: [fill: one design choice and its tradeoff, for example a human review step before a brief reaches the CEO]
long.buy_in: [fill: how you are getting feedback from the executive users]
long.result: The work is ongoing. [fill: the latest progress you can measure and share]
long.different: I would agree the success measure with the executives before building, for example time from an issue appearing to an owner acting on it.
long.at_aws: On AWS I would use Amazon Bedrock for the models, Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases over internal documents, and AWS Lambda tools behind each connector with least-privilege IAM roles, with Amazon Bedrock Guardrails on what reaches the CEO.

stories.title: Human-in-the-loop annotation pipeline
stories.headline: I am building an annotation pipeline that combines rubric-based LLM labels with expert review for lower-confidence caseworker notes.
stories.s: At USC AI Trust Lab, I am using Llama 3.3 70B to label caseworker notes. Annotation needs a consistent definition of each label, and the model needs a path to escalate the cases it cannot handle confidently.
stories.t: My task is to turn that into a pipeline with a rubric, confidence scores, and human-in-the-loop review.
a: I am building the rubric-based labeling workflow on Llama 3.3 70B, giving the annotation process explicit criteria rather than asking the model for an unconstrained answer.
I am adding confidence scoring that routes low-confidence cases to domain experts. The model handles labeling, while the review path brings in human judgment where it matters.
I am keeping the design centered on three responsibilities: produce a label, expose uncertainty, and route the cases that need attention.
stories.r: The work is ongoing. The pipeline labels notes, scores confidence, and routes lower-confidence cases to experts, giving the annotation workflow a concrete path from an initial model label to domain-expert review.
stories.lesson: The design lesson is that confidence should guide review, not stand in for proof that a model is correct. The escalation path belongs in the architecture.
stories.twist: For engineers, explain rubric evaluation, confidence calibration, expert review, and actual data controls. For executives, describe the boundary of model decision-making and what evidence is still needed. Do not claim measured accuracy or reviewer savings without a result.
stories.aws: Proposed AWS design, not a claim of AWS implementation: choose a supported model on Bedrock or deploy a compatible model with SageMaker AI, evaluate on expert-labeled cases, and implement an authenticated human-review workflow with Step Functions Standard callbacks. Add explicit permissions and retention controls; guardrails do not validate factual accuracy. Callback pattern: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/step-functions/latest/dg/connect-to-resource.html.

probes.q: What does the rubric contribute?
probes.a: The rubric gives the Llama 3.3 70B annotation workflow explicit criteria for assigning labels. I built the rubric-based pipeline; that is separate from claiming sole authorship of the domain definitions. For evaluation, I would work with experts on clear label descriptions and examples, test ambiguous cases, and refine the criteria when reviewers disagree.

probes.q: How do you know the labels are good?
probes.a: The implemented workflow scores confidence and routes lower-confidence cases to domain experts. That provides a review path; it is not by itself an accuracy result. I would evaluate expert agreement on a labeled sample, inspect disagreements by category, and also sample high-confidence outputs so confident mistakes are not invisible.

stories.evidence_note: Resume-supported actions and metrics are candidate claims, not independently verified. See the resume and STAR review.

long.stakes: Caseworker notes describe real people. A wrong label can mislead research about how people are served, so the pipeline has to know when it is unsure.
long.obstacle: [fill: the hardest part, for example writing rubric criteria two experts would apply the same way]
long.tradeoff: Routing more cases to experts raises quality but uses scarce expert time. The confidence threshold is the dial between them.
long.buy_in: [fill: how you are working with the domain experts on the rubric]
long.result: The work is ongoing. The pipeline labels notes, scores confidence, and routes low-confidence cases to experts. [fill: any measured progress so far]
long.different: I would measure agreement between the model and the experts on a fixed sample from the start.
long.at_aws: On AWS I would host the model on Amazon Bedrock or Amazon SageMaker AI, use AWS Step Functions to pause low-confidence cases for expert review, and keep the notes in Amazon S3 with strict access controls and encryption.

stories.title: ModelScope quantization study
stories.headline: In ModelScope, my INT4 benchmark used 2299 MB and sustained 13.7 tokens per second with MMLU within a point of baseline.
stories.s: I benchmarked Llama-3.2-3B and Gemma-2-2B on a T4 GPU to understand quantization tradeoffs. A smaller memory footprint is only useful if the model also meets the quality and performance requirements of its workload.
stories.t: My task was to compare configurations across latency, throughput, peak memory, and evaluation quality instead of selecting precision from a single metric.
a: I tested 8 configurations spanning FP16, INT8, INT4, and NF4, using PyTorch and CUDA to profile inference.

I measured the resource and performance dimensions, then used a Pareto sweep to compare tradeoffs. That makes it possible to identify configurations that improve one requirement without ignoring the others.
I included MMLU as a quality check alongside the performance measurements, keeping the conclusion tied to the benchmark setup.
stories.r: INT4 used 2299 MB, 62% below FP16, while sustaining 13.7 tokens per second and keeping MMLU within a point of baseline.
stories.lesson: The lesson is to benchmark the workload before recommending a model configuration, then choose a configuration that meets its quality, performance, and operational requirements.
stories.twist: For engineers, explain the exact model, workload, measurement method, comparator, and quality constraint. For executives, describe the tested resource-versus-quality choice and the need for customer-specific evaluation. No production cost saving or universal precision recommendation is established.
stories.aws: Proposed AWS design, not a claim of AWS implementation: Inferentia or G instances for inference, smaller models on Bedrock, SageMaker AI endpoints sized from a benchmark, not a guess.

probes.q: Why was INT8 slower?
probes.a: My core result is the measured INT4 configuration on the T4, with its memory, throughput, and MMLU tradeoff. I would not generalize an INT8 comparison without the exact comparator and workload. Kernel support, model shape, batch size, and quantization overhead can change the result, so I would inspect the profiling evidence before attributing the cause.

probes.q: Would you ship INT4 to a customer?
probes.a: I would treat this benchmark as a candidate configuration, then evaluate the customer workload. I would measure task quality, memory, throughput, latency, and operational constraints on the intended hardware. Staying within a point on MMLU is useful evidence, but it does not establish that the customer application will meet its quality requirements.

stories.evidence_note: Resume-supported actions and metrics are candidate claims, not independently verified. See the resume and STAR review.

long.stakes: Teams often assume they need a bigger GPU to run a model. If a smaller number format keeps quality, the same model runs on cheaper hardware. I wanted data, not assumptions.
long.obstacle: [fill: what was hard, for example keeping the comparison fair with the same prompts and settings across all 8 configs]
long.tradeoff: Smaller formats save memory but can lose quality, so I measured MMLU alongside speed and memory and compared the options on a Pareto view instead of a single number.
long.buy_in: [fill: whether you shared the results, for example a write-up or repository]
long.result: INT4 used 2299 MB, 62% less than FP16, ran at 13.7 tokens per second, and kept MMLU within a point of baseline. The surprise was INT8: in my setup it used 53% more memory than INT4 and ran 2.1x slower, so it lost on both counts.
long.different: I would add a task-specific quality test next to MMLU, because a general benchmark can hide losses on the task a customer cares about.
long.at_aws: On AWS I would run the same sweep on Amazon EC2 GPU instances and on AWS Inferentia2, compare cost per token, and host the winner on an Amazon SageMaker AI endpoint, or bring it in with Amazon Bedrock Custom Model Import if its architecture is supported.

stories.title: Nightly Databricks feed
stories.headline: I automated a nightly Databricks feed for 17 financial tables and 4.2M rows, with a 22-minute full refresh.
stories.s: At MSRcosmos, the ERP agents depended on financial data from Databricks workspaces across AWS, Azure, and GCP. The data pipeline was part of making the agent workflow useful: the agents needed the underlying records available for processing.
stories.t: My task was to automate the nightly feed and stage the financial tables into Delta Lake.
a: I built the feed with PySpark, bringing the 17 tables and 4.2M rows into Delta Lake.
I used partition pruning to reduce unnecessary reads, and incremental merges to incorporate changes without treating every update as a complete rewrite.

I automated the feed across the cloud workspaces, connecting the data-engineering layer with the multi-agent ERP system. The processing choices addressed how much data the job needed to read and update.
stories.r: The full refresh held at 22 minutes.
stories.lesson: The lesson is that an AI application still depends on its data foundation. Efficient ingestion and clear refresh behavior matter just as much as the agent logic that uses the data.
stories.twist: For engineers, explain merge keys, deletes, late arrivals, correctness, and the meaning of full refresh. For executives, explain the 22-minute reported refresh in relation to the customer freshness requirement once confirmed. Native AWS equivalents remain proposed designs.
stories.aws: Proposed AWS design, not a claim of AWS implementation: Glue or EMR jobs into S3 with Apache Iceberg tables, Athena for queries, Step Functions or MWAA for scheduling.

probes.q: Why incremental merges?
probes.a: Incremental merges let the pipeline incorporate changes rather than rewrite everything for each update, while partition pruning reduces unnecessary reads. The correctness details still matter: a new design needs a reliable merge key, a policy for deletes and late arrivals, and a way to reconcile the output with the source.

probes.q: What would you do if a source workspace were late?
probes.a: The feed covered Databricks workspaces across AWS, Azure, and GCP. For the recovery design, I would make source freshness visible, distinguish complete from partial inputs, retry safely, and agree with the customer whether to delay publication or expose explicitly stale data. That policy must match what the downstream agents can safely do with incomplete inputs.

probes.q: How do full refresh and incremental merges fit together?
probes.a: The 22-minute result is the full-refresh measure. Partition pruning describes reducing reads, while incremental merges describe how changes are applied. They are not interchangeable runtime measures. Before comparing that result with an incremental run, I would match the input snapshot, rows changed, compute size, and definition of when the refresh begins and ends.

stories.evidence_note: Resume-supported actions and metrics are candidate claims, not independently verified. See the resume and STAR review.

long.stakes: The ERP agents were only as good as the data under them. If the nightly feed ran late or partial, the agents worked from stale financials the next morning.
long.obstacle: [fill: what threatened the refresh window, for example a table that kept growing or a slow full rewrite]
long.tradeoff: A full rewrite every night is simple but slow and expensive. Incremental merges are faster, but change detection has to be right. I used incremental merges with partition pruning so the job read and wrote only what changed.
long.buy_in: [fill: who depended on the feed and how you kept them informed]
long.result: The feed moved 17 financial tables and 4.2M rows into Delta Lake every night, and the full refresh held at 22 minutes.
long.different: I would add data quality checks, such as row counts and totals per table, that fail the run loudly instead of passing bad data to the agents.
long.at_aws: On AWS I would run Spark on AWS Glue or Amazon EMR, keep the data in Amazon S3 as Apache Iceberg tables for merges, govern access with the AWS Glue Data Catalog and AWS Lake Formation, and run checks with Amazon Athena.
